lines: You reported difficulties in 13 of 14 areas (Background and goals; Sustaining attention; Organization and time; Starting and finishing tasks; Forgetfulness in daily life; Restlessness and staying with one thing; Acting quickly and patience; Childhood and school years; Different settings; Impact on work or study; Impact on relationships and daily life; Sleep, stress, mood, and health context; Strategies and support).

Your screening was 5/6 (original-0-6), above the threshold where further assessment may be useful.

Several reported everyday areas plus a positive screen is the kind of presentation an ADHD assessment would explore — but the same pattern can come from many other things, and this sketch is unvalidated.
Only a qualified clinician can determine what explains your experiences. Take both reports to your appointment.

statements.answer: After the warning at work and finding those school reports, I need a proper understanding of what I am dealing with. I have coped my way here on effort and scaffolding, and it is not holding anymore.
statements.question: What brings you to this assessment now, and is there anything about your background you think is relevant?

statements.answer: My attention is either everywhere or hyperglued to the wrong thing. In a normal meeting I am gone within minutes, but I can lose four hours to reorganising my music library without noticing. There is no middle setting.
statements.question: Think about an ordinary day. What is it like for you to stay focused on one thing?

statements.answer: I am the most organised disorganised person you will meet. Colour-coded lists, three apps, reminders for my reminders — and things still fall through the cracks the moment a week gets busy. The system is load-bearing and it still is not enough.
statements.question: How do you find organizing your time, your tasks, or your belongings?

statements.answer: I work long hours to compensate for how slowly things start. I will sit down to do a task and somehow an hour passes before I have begun — tidying, emails, anything but the thing. Then I stay late to catch up, every week.
statements.question: What kinds of tasks are hardest for you to start or finish?

statements.answer: I forget what I walked into rooms for, I forget to reply for days, I forget appointments I made myself. Very often, not occasionally — it is the texture of my days, not an exception.
statements.question: Do you ever forget appointments, obligations, or where you put things? What is that like?

statements.answer: I am restless in the chair sense — shifting, crossing and uncrossing, getting up for water I do not want. Long car journeys are the worst; I arrive feeling like I have run a marathon while sitting down.
statements.question: When you need to sit still or stay with one thing, what is that like for you?

statements.answer: Sometimes I speak before the thought is finished, especially when I am tired. And I say yes to things — projects, favours, trips — before checking whether I have any room for them. My calendar pays the price.
statements.question: How are you with waiting your turn, or holding back when you want to jump in?

statements.answer: Clearing out my parents' loft, I found my old school reports, and it was like reading a preview: constant daydreaming, unfinished work, 'must learn to check his work'. I had forgotten all of it until I saw it in their handwriting.
statements.question: Thinking back to childhood and school, what do you remember about yourself as a child?

statements.answer: It has followed me through every stage — school, university, every job. Whether it was there before I was ten, I cannot recall; my memories that far back are thin. But from my teens onward, it is one continuous thread.
statements.question: How have these kinds of experiences changed over the years, as far as you can tell?

statements.answer: Work shows it most brutally because the stakes are formal. But it is in the small hours of home life too — the unanswered messages, the half-done chores, the plans I forget I made. No setting is exempt.
statements.question: Are these experiences different depending on where you are — for example at home versus work or study?

statements.answer: I got a written warning this year for missed deadlines, despite working longer hours than anyone on the team. That was the moment I stopped telling myself hard work would fix it — the hard work was already happening.
statements.question: Can you describe a recent time when these experiences affected your work or studies?

statements.answer: My partner has started keeping a shared calendar for us because I kept forgetting plans we had made together. They are frustrated, and I do not blame them — being half-listened to for years would wear anyone down.
statements.question: How do these experiences affect the people around you, or your day-to-day life outside work?

statements.answer: Tiredness sharpens everything, and I run tired most weeks because of the late working. But I have had rested holidays where I still forgot the same kinds of things, so rest is not the root of it — it just turns the volume up.
statements.question: Are there things like sleep, stress, mood, or health that seem to make these experiences better or worse?

statements.answer: The lists, the alarms, the shared calendar, body-doubling with a friend over video while we both do admin — I have built scaffolding around my entire life. It holds on good weeks. On bad weeks I walk around the scaffolding instead of using it.
statements.question: What do you do to cope with or work around these experiences — routines, reminders, help from others?

statements.answer: I want something I can show my manager that is honest — not an excuse, an explanation, and ideally a plan. That is what I am hoping this process gives me.
statements.question: What brings you to this assessment now, and is there anything about your background you think is relevant?

statements.answer: The hyperfocus side almost makes it worse, because people see me concentrate intensely on something pointless and conclude I could do it for work if I tried.
statements.question: Think about an ordinary day. What is it like for you to stay focused on one thing?

statements.answer: Maintaining the system is practically a part-time job. I spend Sunday evenings planning the week and by Wednesday the plan is decorative.
statements.question: How do you find organizing your time, your tasks, or your belongings?

statements.answer: The overtime is the hidden tax. My timesheets look heroic and my evenings do not exist. Nobody sees the hour of circling before each task.
statements.question: What kinds of tasks are hardest for you to start or finish?

statements.answer: I once forgot my own birthday dinner — the one I had organised. My friends still bring it up. I laugh along because the alternative is crying.
statements.question: Do you ever forget appointments, obligations, or where you put things? What is that like?

statements.answer: I volunteer for the tea round in long meetings just to have a reason to stand up. People think I am being nice. I am managing my legs.
statements.question: When you need to sit still or stay with one thing, what is that like for you?
